items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 5, 2026
items.excerpt: 05 November 2026• Update: 05 November 2026 WASHINGTON Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Thursday, including US President Donald Trump defending the Iran war amid midterm losses, world leaders offering mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in US midterm elections, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps saying two oil tankers and a tugboat catching fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump said the war in Iran was worth the political and economic costs as his Republic Party lost the midterm elections, insisting that the country had "no choice" but to take military action to prevent Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Asked at the White House whether he believed the conflict was worth it, Trump responded: “I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice.” “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he added. Asked about Vice President JD Vance's suggestion that the war in Iran contributed to Republican losses, Trump agreed, acknowledging that the conflict had pushed gasoline prices higher in the short term. “Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up,” he said. Meanwhile Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections, saying voter anger over the conflict drove former Trump supporters to back Democrats. - World leaders offer mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in US midterm elections World leaders on Wednesday offered mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections, with some welcoming the outcome as a sign of political change while others reaffirming their commitment to maintaining strong relations with Washington. Democrats secured control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's elections, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on their "historic victory" but stressed that Europe must continue assuming greater responsibility for its own security. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez interpreted the outcome as a rejection of Trump's policies and a broader setback for the international far right. French Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the Democrats' electoral gains as "undeniable" but cautioned that Trump would retain significant authority over US foreign policy. British Health Minister James Frith described the results as a "seismic shift" in US domestic politics but said the change would not affect the longstanding relationship between London and Washington. European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose expressed cautious optimism that the Democratic victory could benefit Ukraine, the green transition and international cooperation. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning described the elections as an internal American affair and reiterated Beijing's willingness to maintain constructive relations with Washington. South Africa, President Cyril Ramaphosa welcomed the reported Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, interpreting the results as a clear expression of the American electorate's preferences. - Iran says 3 vessels catch fire in Strait of Hormuz Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Thursday said that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz after vessels attempted to use what it called an unauthorized route. In a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency, the Revolutionary Guard said a large oil tanker struck a mine Wednesday night while attempting to pass through an “unauthorized route” south of the strait. The tanker caught fire and came to a halt, the statement said. In a separate incident, another supertanker caught fire while leaving the route in the eastern part of the strait, it said. A tugboat approaching to help extinguish the blaze also caught fire, the statement added. The Revolutionary Guard also said that its navy's electronic warfare unit had "taken control of two Lucas-type aircraft" that it described as "intruding." The Revolutionary Guard claimed that its navy continued to maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: US services sector activity cools slightly in October; inflation remains elevated By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 04, 2026, 10:08 AM Updated Nov 04, 2026, 10:12 AM ... WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - US services sector growth slowed marginally in October amid a moderation in new orders, but supply chains remained strained, keeping prices for inputs elevated. The Institute for Supply Management said on Wednesday its nonmanufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index dipped to 54.5 last month from 54.9 in September. A reading above 50 indicates growth in the services sector, which accounts for more than two-thirds of US economic activity. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI little changed at 54.8. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing, though economists expect a slowdown in activity, with consumer spending expected to pull back after back-to-back quarters of robust growth. Spending is seen in part curbed by high inflation, which is eroding household purchasing power. Income at the disposal of households, after adjusting for inflation and taxes, fell in September after being unchanged in August. The saving rate is at a four-year low of 3.8%. The survey’s measure of new orders received by services businesses decreased to 55.9 last month from 59.8 in September. Delivery performance by suppliers deteriorated further against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and tariffs on imports. The Middle East conflict, now in its ninth month, has boosted energy prices and caused shortages of commodities that are shipped through the Strait of Hormuz. The survey’s measure of supplier deliveries jumped to 56.7 from 53.2 in September. A reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. Deliveries have slowed for 23 consecutive months, keeping input prices high. The survey’s measure of prices paid by businesses for inputs eased to a still-high 73.0 last month from 74.0 in September. The ISM on Monday reported a slight moderation in prices paid for inputs by manufacturers in October. Economists expect inflation to continue to run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target into 2027. The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the US central bank to raise borrowing costs in December. The ISM survey showed a marginal increase in services sector employment, aligning with economists’ expectations for moderate growth in nonfarm payrolls in October. The survey’s measure of services employment rose to 51.4 from 50.1 in September. The government’s closely watched employment report on Friday is likely to show payrolls advanced by 65,000 in October after increasing 29,000 in September, according to a Reuters survey of economists. The unemployment rate is forecast to have been unchanged at 4.2%.

items.title: Oil falls for a fourth day on expectations for lower risk of Iran war escalation
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 12:02 AM EST Oil prices fell for a fourth day on Thursday on expectations the losses U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered in Congressional elections this week may reduce the risk of further escalation of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Todd Korol | Reuters Oil prices fell for a fourth day on Thursday on expectations the losses U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered in Congressional elections this week may reduce the risk of further escalation of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent futures Add To Watchlist fell 97 cents, or 1.03% at $93.65 a barrel as of 0211 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures Add To Watchlist were down $1.14, or 1.29%, to $86.98. Both benchmarks tumbled by more than 8% in the previous session to settle at their lowest since August 31. A weakened Trump, facing a Democratic Congress able to constrain his military options, has greater incentive to seek a deal, two sources close to Gulf government circles said on Wednesday. A full-scale assault on Iran now looks less likely, they said. A resolution to the conflict could restore oil flows from the Middle East impacted by the war, though analysts caution the way forward remains uncertain. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections to Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," said June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities. "However, there will be more volatility ahead as the path to full diplomacy to end the war is still wrought with many unknowns while the global strategic reserves have drawn very thin." Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz — the key waterway for most Gulf oil supplies — have recovered to close to pre-war levels, according to analysts, though at a higher cost. The resumption of Gulf supply has pushed the global oil market back into surplus after months of disruption caused by the war, JPMorgan said in a note on Wednesday. JPMorgan estimates the market returned to a surplus of 1.1 million barrels per day in September, widening to 1.4 million bpd in October, nearly matching last year's average of 1.3 million bpd. Still, the sharp selloff in oil may prove short-lived. "The short answer is no," said Mukesh Sahdev, CEO of energy consultancy XAnalysts, when asked whether prices were likely to remain lower after the election. Sahdev said geopolitical risks remained difficult to predict and noted the incoming Congress would not take office until January, meaning US policy options had not immediately changed. He also noted commercial oil inventories in major consuming countries are near their lowest in 15 years and said Iran could emerge from the US election outcome with greater resolve. US crude, gasoline and distillate inventories all fell last week as demand hit its highest in a year, the Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday.

items.title: The Latest: Trump defends Iran war after voters give Democrats control of Congress – NewsNation
items.excerpt: The midterm election blowout has set up a new era in Washington, with Democrats eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their congressional majorities evaporate in a revolt against President Donald Trump’s policies. Democrats triumphed in several surprise upsets, marking a decisive rejection of unified GOP control of the House and Senate. Trump acknowledged the Iran war affected the midterms, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the more than 8-month-old conflict. “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters. He struck a conciliatory tone earlier, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, only to later threaten to use his veto power to strike down their agenda. The fallout for Republicans is only beginning. Vice President JD Vance, a 2028 presidential contender, blamed the war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout. And Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House speaker, according to two people familiar with the matter. Democrats, meanwhile, are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.

Prior to the election, Republicans held the majority in the chamber, 53-47. - Republicans have managed to flip one seat in Texas' 32nd congressional district. items.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
items.excerpt: Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run. In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election. "The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night." In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate. Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials. But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now. Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran? Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said. It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue. Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices. It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign. "I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon." Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. ... Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel." The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech. ... Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over. It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
